questions.prompt: Why does a password reset fail to remediate a stolen certificate?
options: Because certificates are stored in the SYSVOL share
Because a certificate remains valid until it expires -- typically one or two years -- independent of the account's password
Because password resets do not replicate to the CA
questions.explanation: Certificate validity is tied to its expiry and revocation status, not the account password. This is why revocation, not credential rotation, is the required remediation.

questions.prompt: What combination of settings makes a certificate template ESC1-vulnerable?
options: Any template that includes a client authentication EKU
Enrollee-supplied subject, a client authentication EKU, broad enrollment rights, and no manager approval required
A template published to more than one CA
A template with a validity period over one year
questions.explanation: All four conditions together let any permitted enrollee request a certificate naming an arbitrary identity in the SAN and have the CA issue it -- no exploit required.

questions.prompt: Why can an ESC4 attack evade a point-in-time template audit?
options: Because template changes are never logged
Because the attacker can reconfigure a template, exploit it, then revert the change -- leaving the current state clean and the evidence only in change events
Because ESC4 does not involve templates at all
Because certificate templates cannot be audited
questions.explanation: With write access over the template object, the misconfiguration exists only briefly. An audit of current state afterward shows nothing, so detection depends on 5136 change events or replication metadata.

questions.prompt: In an ESC8 attack, why is a certificate for a domain controller machine account so damaging?
options: It leads to a TGT for that DC, and from there to DCSync and the full credential database
It only permits reading public DNS records
It grants access to the CA's web interface only
questions.explanation: A certificate authenticating as a DC computer account yields a TGT for that DC, which carries the replication rights needed to run DCSync against the entire domain.
